provenance_chain.statement_summary: The clavicle is classified morphologically as a long bone.
The clavicle forms the anterior component of the pectoral girdle.
The clavicle is a bilateral paired bone.
The clavicle is situated in the anterosuperior part of the thorax, between sternum and scapula.
The clavicle possesses an elongated double curvature resembling an italic S.
The medial two-thirds of the clavicle is convex anteriorly.
The lateral one-third of the clavicle is concave anteriorly.
The clavicle presents a central body or shaft.
The clavicle possesses an expanded medial sternal extremity.
The clavicle possesses a flattened lateral acromial extremity.
The clavicle has a superior surface.
The clavicle has an inferior surface.
The clavicle presents an anterior border.
The clavicle presents a posterior border.
The middle portion of the superior surface of the clavicle is smooth and subcutaneous.
The inferior surface presents the impression for the costoclavicular ligament at its medial end.
The middle third of the inferior surface contains the longitudinal subclavian groove.
The lateral third of the inferior surface exhibits the conoid tubercle near its posterior border.
The lateral third of the inferior surface presents the trapezoid line running anterolaterally from the conoid tubercle.
The inferior surface features the principal nutrient foramen directed laterally towards the acromial end.
The sternal end of the clavicle bears the sternal articular surface.
The sternal articular facet articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium and the first costal cartilage.
The acromial end of the clavicle bears the acromial articular surface.
The acromial articular facet articulates with the medial articular facet of the acromion of the scapula.
The clavicular head of pectoralis major originates from the anterior border and adjacent superior surface of the medial two-thirds of the clavicle.
The clavicular portion of the deltoid muscle originates from the anterior border and superior surface of the lateral one-third of the clavicle.
The descending part of the trapezius inserts into the posterior border and adjacent superior surface of the lateral one-third of the clavicle.
The clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle originates from the posterosuperior aspect of the medial third of the clavicle.
The subclavius muscle inserts into the subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the clavicle.
The costoclavicular ligament attaches to the costoclavicular impression on the inferior surface of the sternal end.
The conoid ligament attaches to the conoid tubercle on the inferior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle.
The trapezoid ligament attaches to the trapezoid line on the inferior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle.
The clavicle consists of a thick outer cortical layer of compact bone enclosing a cancellous core without a true continuous medullary cavity.
The clavicle is subcutaneous and palpable in living humans throughout its entire length from sternum to acromion.
Fibers of the platysma muscle cross subcutaneously superficial to the superior surface of the clavicle.
The medial, intermediate, and lateral supraclavicular nerves cross superficial to the clavicle within subcutaneous tissue.
The subclavian vein and subclavian artery pass directly deep to the middle third of the clavicle above the first rib.
The trunks and divisions of the brachial plexus pass posteroinferior to the middle third of the clavicle into the axilla.
The clavicle is oriented in space by placing the flattened acromial end laterally, the smooth surface superiorly, and the anterior convexity of the larger curve medially.

Laterality is determined by confirming that the bulbous sternal end is medial, the rough ligamentous ridges (conoid tubercle, trapezoid line) are on the inferior surface, and the lateral curve is concave anteriorly.
The anterior border of the lateral third frequently presents a small projection known as the deltoid tubercle.
The clavicle is the first bone in the human skeleton to begin ossification (around the 5th to 6th embryonic week), primarily via intramembranous ossification with endochondral ends.
The secondary epiphysis of the sternal end appears late (18-20 years) and is the last long bone epiphysis to fuse with the shaft (around age 25).
The clavipectoral fascia splits to envelop the subclavius muscle, attaching firmly to the anterior and posterior margins of the subclavian groove.
The nutrient artery of the clavicle typically arises from the suprascapular artery or thoracoacromial artery and enters through the nutrient foramen.
The posterior border of the clavicle is concave in its medial two-thirds and convex in its lateral third.
The anterior border of the clavicle is convex in its medial two-thirds and concave in its lateral third.
The investing layer of deep cervical fascia attaches to the superior surface and posterior border of the clavicle.
The junction between the convex medial two-thirds and concave lateral one-third of the clavicle represents the structural point of greatest mechanical stress and curvature transition.
Unlike typical tubular long bones, the clavicular shaft lacks a true well-defined central medullary cavity throughout life.
Sensory and periosteal innervation to the clavicle is supplied principally by twigs from the nerve to the subclavius and supraclavicular nerves.
The posterior border of the clavicle forms the inferior boundary of the greater supraclavicular fossa (omoclavicular triangle).
The sternoclavicular joint is anatomically classified as a synovial saddle (sellar / encaje recíproco) joint.
The sternoclavicular joint connects the pectoral girdle directly to the axial skeleton.
The articular surfaces are the sternal end of the clavicle, the clavicular notch of the manubrium sterni, and the superior aspect of the first costal cartilage.
The articulating bony surfaces of the sternoclavicular joint are covered with fibrocartilage rather than typical hyaline cartilage.
The sternoclavicular joint contains a complete interarticular fibrocartilaginous disc.
Superiorly, the articular disc is attached to the posterosuperior border of the sternal articular surface of the clavicle.
Inferiorly, the articular disc is attached to the junction between the first costal cartilage and the sternum.
The articular disc completely partitions the joint space into meniscoclavicular (superolateral) and meniscosternal (inferomedial) synovial cavities.
The joint is surrounded by a fibrous capsule that attaches around the periphery of the articular surfaces and disc.
The fibrous capsule is reinforced anteriorly by the anterior sternoclavicular ligament.
The fibrous capsule is reinforced posteriorly by the posterior sternoclavicular ligament, which is thicker and stronger than the anterior ligament.
The superior aspect of the joint is strengthened by the interclavicular ligament bridging across the jugular notch.
The joint is powerfully stabilized extracapsularly by the costoclavicular ligament.
The costoclavicular ligament arises from the superior surface of the first rib and adjacent first costal cartilage.
The costoclavicular ligament serves as the primary restraint against upward displacement (elevation) of the clavicle and limits anterior/posterior translation.
The sternoclavicular joint permits elevation of approximately 30° to 45° and depression of approximately 5° to 10°.
The sternoclavicular joint permits anterior protraction of 15° to 20° and posterior retraction of 20° to 30°.
The sternoclavicular joint accommodates axial rotation of the clavicle up to 30° to 40° along its longitudinal axis during full arm abduction.
Arterial blood supply to the sternoclavicular joint is derived from branches of the internal thoracic artery and the suprascapular artery.
The sternoclavicular joint receives articular sensory innervation from the medial supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4) and the nerve to the subclavius (C5, C6).
The posterior ligament and joint capsule lie immediately anterior to the confluence of the internal jugular and subclavian veins forming the brachiocephalic vein.
The retrosternoclavicular space relates posteriorly to the brachiocephalic trunk on the right side and common carotid artery on the left side.
The interclavicular ligament tightens during downward movement of the shoulder, preventing excessive depression of the acromial end of the clavicle.
The sternoclavicular joint forms an easily palpable subcutaneous elevation on each side of the jugular notch of the manubrium.
Because of its wedge-shaped attachments, the articular disc resists upward and medial displacement of the clavicle when axial loads are transmitted from the shoulder.
The posterior surface of the SC capsule is directly cushioned by the origins of the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles separating it from retrosternal veins.
Anterior subluxation occurs more frequently than posterior dislocation due to the greater strength of the posterior sternoclavicular ligament and costoclavicular complex.
The costoclavicular ligament exhibits an anterior lamina directed superolaterally and a posterior lamina directed superomedially, forming an inverted cone.
The acromioclavicular joint is classified anatomically as a synovial plane joint (arthrodia).
The acromioclavicular joint unites the lateral extremity of the clavicle to the scapular spine continuation (acromion).
The joint articulates the oval facet on the acromial end of the clavicle with the complementary facet on the medial margin of the acromion.
The clavicular acromial facet is beveled to face downward and outward (inferolaterally).
The acromial articular facet of the scapula is beveled to face upward and inward (superomedially).
Both articular surfaces of the acromioclavicular joint are lined with fibrocartilage.
The AC joint frequently possesses a wedge-shaped fibrocartilaginous disc (meniscoid) hanging into the upper joint cavity.
The acromioclavicular disc is often incomplete, wedge-like, or absent in older adult populations.
The joint is enveloped by a relatively thin fibrous capsule attached around the articular margins.
The joint capsule is reinforced by the acromioclavicular ligament, which exhibits distinct superior and inferior bands.
The superior acromioclavicular ligament is a robust quadrilateral band intermingled with aponeurotic fibers of the trapezius and deltoid muscles.
The superior acromioclavicular ligament provides primary resistance against horizontal and anteroposterior displacement of the AC joint.
Movements at the acromioclavicular joint consist of subtle gliding and rotations that allow the scapula to maintain apposition with the curving thoracic wall during arm elevation.
The AC joint allows variation of the angle formed between the clavicle and the scapular spine (opening and closing of the scapuloclavicular angle).
Vascular supply to the AC joint is derived from the acromial arterial network formed by the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery and the suprascapular artery.
The acromioclavicular joint receives articular innervation from the lateral supraclavicular nerve, axillary nerve, and lateral pectoral nerve.
The joint line of the acromioclavicular articulation is palpable subcutaneously approximately 2 to 3 cm medial to the lateral border of the acromion.
In normal surface anatomy, the lateral end of the clavicle projects slightly superior to the acromion, forming a small palpable step.
The synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule and covers any intracapsular portion of the articular disc.
The inclined planes of the acromial and clavicular articular facets render the joint mechanically prone to superior dislocation of the clavicle under downward direct impact on the acromion.
The acromioclavicular joint capsule lies immediately superior to the lateral attachment of the coracoacromial ligament on the acromion.
With advancing age, degenerative remodeling, fibrocartilage fraying, and narrowing of the acromioclavicular joint space are standard physiological findings.
The coracoclavicular ligament complex is an extrinsic syndesmotic ligamentous apparatus uniting the coracoid process of the scapula to the inferior aspect of the clavicle.
The complex consists of two distinct anatomically and functionally differentiated ligaments: the conoid ligament and the trapezoid ligament.
The conoid ligament is the posteromedial component of the coracoclavicular complex.
The conoid ligament is shaped like an inverted triangle or cone with an inferior apex and a superior base.
The apex of the conoid ligament originates from the medial and posterior aspect of the base of the coracoid process of the scapula.
The diverging fibers of the conoid ligament insert into the conoid tubercle on the inferior surface of the clavicle.
The conoid ligament acts as the primary restraint against superior translation of the clavicle relative to the scapula and limits anterior tilting of the scapula.
The trapezoid ligament is the anterolateral component of the coracoclavicular complex.
The trapezoid ligament is a thick, flat, quadrilateral fibrous plate oriented in an oblique anterolateral plane.
The inferior border of the trapezoid ligament arises from the upper surface of the horizontal segment of the coracoid process.
The superior border of the trapezoid ligament inserts along the oblique trapezoid line on the inferior surface of the clavicle.
The trapezoid ligament primarily restrains posterior displacement of the clavicle and resists horizontal approximation or axial override of the clavicle across the acromion.
The coracoclavicular ligament complex provides the primary passive suspensory mechanism suspending the scapula and upper limb from the clavicular strut.
The conoid and trapezoid ligaments meet posteriorly at their coracoid bases and diverge laterally and anteriorly, forming an angle occupied by fatty areolar tissue or an interligamentous bursa.
The coracoclavicular ligaments receive microvascular supply from descending branches of the suprascapular and thoracoacromial arteries.
Articular proprioceptive innervation to the coracoclavicular complex is supplied by fine branches of the suprascapular nerve.
An accessory medial coracoclavicular band (ligament of Caldani / bicorne) is occasionally present running from the coracoid base to the first rib or subclavius sheath.
The conoid ligament fibers are oriented predominantly in a coronal vertical plane.
The trapezoid ligament fibers are oriented in a subhorizontal, anterolaterally oblique plane.
The coracoid attachment of the conoid ligament lies immediately anterior to the suprascapular notch and the superior transverse scapular ligament.
Tightening of the conoid ligament during scapular upward rotation pulls on the conoid tubercle, forcing passive posterior rotation of the clavicle.
Rupture of both conoid and trapezoid ligaments abolishes vertical scapular suspension, producing classic high-grade acromioclavicular dislocation (piano key sign).
The pectoral girdle (cingulum pectorale) is the musculoskeletal ring connecting the upper limbs to the axial trunk.
The skeletal framework of each half of the pectoral girdle is formed solely by the clavicle anteriorly and the scapula posterolaterally.
The pectoral girdle is closed anteriorly by the manubrium of the sternum but remains widely open posteriorly, where the scapulae are connected only by muscular slings.
The sternoclavicular joint represents the sole true anatomical synovial articulation anchoring the upper extremity to the axial skeleton.
The clavicle functions mechanically as a rigid bony strut (brace) that holds the scapula and shoulder joint laterally away from the thoracic wall, maximizing free arm mobility.

Mechanical compressive forces pass from the hand and humerus to the glenoid cavity, through the scapula to the coracoclavicular ligaments, along the clavicle to the costoclavicular ligament and sternoclavicular joint, and into the sternum.
The pectoral girdle incorporates the scapulothoracic functional interface (syssarcosis) as a critical component of shoulder girdle kinematics.
The scapulothoracic articulation is not a true anatomical synovial or fibrous joint, but a physiological syssarcosis formed by muscular gliding planes.
The serratus anterior muscle forms the intermediate fleshy partition dividing the scapulothoracic interface into two distinct gliding spaces.
The omo-serratus (scapulo-serratus) space lies between the subscapularis fascia lining the costal surface of the scapula and the lateral surface of the serratus anterior.
The parieto-serratus (thoraco-serratus) space lies between the medial surface of the serratus anterior and the posterolateral rib cage (ribs 2-7 and intercostal muscles).

The scapulothoracic interface accommodates translational movements (elevation/depression, protraction/retraction) and rotational movements (upward/downward rotation around a physiological sagittal axis).

In full arm abduction (180°), approximately 120° occurs at the glenohumeral joint and 60° occurs through synchronous rotation of the pectoral girdle (scapulothoracic, sternoclavicular, and acromioclavicular joints).
The anterosuperior aspect of the pectoral girdle presents the deltopectoral groove.
The deltopectoral groove is an intermuscular furrow separating the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles.
The deltopectoral groove is bounded medially by the clavicular head of the pectoralis major and laterally by the anterior border of the deltoid.
Near the clavicle, the groove widens into the deltopectoral (clavipectoral / Mohrenheim) triangle bounded superiorly by the clavicle.
The deltopectoral groove lodges and transmits the cephalic vein and the deltoid artery (branch of thoracoacromial trunk).
The skeletal framework of the pectoral girdle forms the boundaries of the cervicoaxillary canal.
The cervicoaxillary canal is bounded anteriorly by the posterior surface of the clavicle, posterolaterally by the superior border of the scapula, and medially by the outer border of the first rib.
The cervicoaxillary canal transmits the subclavian/axillary vessels and the cords of the brachial plexus from the root of the neck into the apex of the axilla.
The pectoral girdle defines the surgically critical retroclavicular space.
The subclavius muscle and its surrounding clavipectoral sheath act as a dynamic muscular cushion protecting the underlying subclavian vein and artery from bone fragments during clavicular trauma.

Motion of the pectoral girdle is powered by anterior axioappendicular muscles (pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, subclavius, serratus anterior) and posterior axioappendicular muscles (trapezius, levator scapulae, rhomboids, latissimus dorsi).
Upward rotation of the scapula is driven by a coordinated force couple between the upper and lower trapezius fibers and the lower digitations of the serratus anterior.
At the apex of the deltopectoral groove, the cephalic vein pierces the clavipectoral fascia within Mohrenheim triangle to drain into the axillary vein.
In multi-axis high-speed kinematic models, clavicular rotation follows an instantaneous spatial helical screw axis rather than fixed planar coordinates.
The gliding tissue between serratus anterior and chest wall demonstrates hyaluronic acid-rich adventitial micro-bursal lubricating films under physiological conditions.
